Prediction-Error Criteria for the Hyperparameters

Source: R/outer_criteria.R
aic.Rd

Build the object that specifies, for statmod(), that a model's hyperparameters are chosen by an estimate of prediction error. Pass the result as outer_criterion for the smooth hyperparameters, as sparse_criterion for a lasso's or a SCAD's, or as both.

The criterion is $$C(\theta) = -2\ell(\hat\beta(\theta)) + \kappa\,\tau(\theta),$$ with \(\tau = \mathrm{tr}[(H+S)^{-1}H]\) the effective degrees of freedom and \(\kappa\) the price of one of them. aic() charges 2 by default and bic() charges \(\log n\), with \(n\) the number of observations (the total of the weights, which are frequencies). Both are minimized.

Usage

aic(k = 2, information = observed_info())

bic(information = observed_info())

Arguments

k

The price of one degree of freedom, a single non-negative finite number. Defaults to 2, which is Akaike's. k = log(n) by hand is bic(). A value that is not a single non-negative finite number is an error. bic() does not take it: its \(\kappa\) is NA on the object and is resolved to \(\log n\) when the model is fitted, because the sample size is unknown until then.

information

The information on which the criterion is built, an object that inherits from distributions7::Information: distributions7::observed_info() (the default) or distributions7::expected_info(), whose method is NULL (the closed form of the family where it has one, and distributions7::expect_opg() otherwise) or one of distributions7::expect_opg(), distributions7::expect_integrate() and distributions7::expect_mc() (see distributions7::expected_derivative_methods). auto_info() is not admissible, since the effective degrees of freedom are the trace on one named matrix, and signals an error. The exact gradient is available on either matrix; the Hessian is exact on the observed one and is not available on the expected one, where the search uses an optimizer that needs only the gradient. On the expected information, the method object defines the matrix and the derivative of it that the gradient reads, as described for the information of reml(). With method = NULL on a family without a closed form, the matrix is the distributions7::expect_opg() estimate of the expected information, noisier than a computed expectation and about 25 times cheaper (0.8 s against 25.3 s for method = expect_integrate(identity = "score") on a density-only family with n = 300); the computed expectation is selected with that method. information_objects compares the objects.

Value

An OuterMethod() object with properties kind ("aic" or "bic"), hessian (the object given as information), k (the number given, or NA_real_ for bic()), marginal (NULL), and the path settings nfolds, rule and folds, which only cv() reads.

Marginal and prediction-error criteria

reml() and ml() integrate the coefficients out and maximize what is left, which needs a penalty that is twice differentiable at the mode. A kinked penalty puts the mode on the kink for every coefficient that it sets to zero, where the penalized information does not exist. A marginal criterion therefore leaves the coordinates that such a penalty covers out of its determinant and does not select the hyperparameter of the kinked penalty. These two criteria select it, and bic() is statmod()'s default sparse_criterion.

For a smooth penalty both families apply. A marginal criterion selects the hyperparameter that makes the data most likely after the coefficients are integrated out, and these select the one that predicts best.

Exact derivatives

The derivatives follow from the implicit function theorem, using the same pieces as the marginal criteria. The envelope theorem does not apply here: \(\ell\) alone is not stationary at the penalized mode, so its derivative carries \(d\hat\beta/d\theta\) from the first order. This is computable because of the mode's own condition, \(\partial\ell/\partial\beta = \partial\rho/\partial\beta\).

The gradient is exact with either information. The Hessian is exact with information = observed_info(), which is the default, and is not available with distributions7::expected_info().

Which effective degrees of freedom

The trace runs over the whole coefficient vector, so a term's contribution reads the full penalized information, including the term's couplings with the other blocks. statmod_edf() reads each term's share from the diagonal block of the same full smoother matrix \((H+S)^{-1}H\), so the per-term numbers add up to \(\tau\). The count stored in the fitted model (fit@edf) is read on the information of this criterion, so that it reproduces the \(\tau\) that the criterion charged, and summary.StatmodFit() keeps it whatever its vcov_type is. For a positive semidefinite \(H\) the total lies in \([0, p]\), with \(p\) the number of coefficients; an indefinite observed information can give a direction of negative curvature a negative share.

Where a penalty has a kink the trace is restricted to the active coordinates, so for a lasso \(\tau\) is the number of surviving coefficients, the unbiased count of Zou, Hastie and Tibshirani (2007).

GCV is not offered

Classical GCV divides a residual sum of squares by \((n-\tau)^2\), which estimates an unknown scale. Here every distribution parameter carries its own equation and the fit profiles no parameter, so there is no unknown scale for that ratio to estimate and the criterion degenerates to aic(). That is the substitution that Wood (2008) makes in the other direction when the scale is known.

A GCV on the squared error of the fitted mean is a different and well-defined object. It would need the derivative of that mean in the parameters, which is not one of distributions7's generics.

Kinked penalties

The penalized mode is only piecewise smooth in such a hyperparameter, turning a corner whenever a coefficient joins the active set or leaves it, so the criterion inherits the corners and is swept over a grid. How the path covers a term carrying more than one kinked hyperparameter belongs to the term, through modelterms7::term_search(). The same criterion object also selects the model's smooth hyperparameters, which are not swept.

References

Zou, H., Hastie, T. and Tibshirani, R. (2007). On the degrees of freedom of the lasso. The Annals of Statistics 35(5), 2173–2192.

Wood, S. N. (2008). Fast stable direct fitting and smoothness selection for generalized additive models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 70(3), 495–518.

See also

reml() and ml() for the marginal criteria, cv() for cross-validation, statmod() for where these are passed.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(200, -2, 2))
dd$y <- sin(1.4 * dd$x) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.3)

fa <- statmod(y ~ s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)), distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd,
              outer_criterion = aic())
fb <- statmod(y ~ s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)), distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd,
              outer_criterion = bic())

# BIC charges log(n) = 5.3 per degree of freedom against AIC's 2, so it
# buys a smoother fit: a larger smoothing parameter and fewer edf.
c(aic = unlist(fa@hyper), bic = unlist(fb@hyper))
#> aic.mu.s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)).lambda 
#>                                  0.5696677 
#> bic.mu.s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)).lambda 
#>                                 13.4428649 
c(aic = sum(fa@edf$edf), bic = sum(fb@edf$edf))
#>      aic      bic 
#> 9.914632 7.258561 

# The object is a specification and carries no data.
aic()
#> <AIC>  observed information
aic(k = 4)@k
#> [1] 4
